questions.title: In OFT, what exactly counts as a "neuron" in the weight matrix $\bm{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the OFT paper, and for a fully connected layer they write $\bm{W} = \{\bm{w}_1, \ldots, \bm{w}_n\} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$ with output $\bm{z} = \bm{W}^\top \bm{x}$. So it seems each column $\bm{w}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is called a neuron. My confusion is that many implementations store linear weights in the opposite shape, and for convolution or attention layers it is even less obvious what the "neuron" object is. When the paper says it preserves pairwise relationships among neurons, should I interpret that as preserving angles between output-channel weight vectors, attention projection columns, or something else?

questions.title: Why does left-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserve pairwise neuron angles and hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: The main OFT update is $\bm{W} = \bm{R} \bm{W}^0$ with $\bm{R}^\top \bm{R} = \bm{I}$. The paper says this provably preserves the pairwise hyperspherical similarity between neurons in the same layer, and therefore preserves the hyperspherical energy. I think this should follow from orthogonal matrices preserving inner products and norms, but I am not fully seeing the derivation when the energy is defined as $\mathrm{HE}(\bm{W}) = \sum_{i \ne j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. Can someone show explicitly why $\hat{\bm{w}}_i = \bm{R}\hat{\bm{w}}_i^0$ implies each pairwise term stays unchanged?

questions.title: If OFT applies the same orthogonal transform to all neurons in a layer, why is it not just a change of basis?
questions.question_body: I may be misunderstanding something basic. If every neuron in a layer is transformed by the same orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$, then it feels like we are just rotating the coordinate system. In linear algebra, a pure change of basis usually should not change the represented function if the rest of the network is adjusted consistently. But OFT only changes one layer to $\bm{W} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0$, and the paper claims this meaningfully changes generation behavior. What is the right intuition here? Is OFT functionally equivalent to rotating the input features to that layer by $\bm{R}^\top$, or is there a better way to think about why the model output changes?

questions.title: How strong is the connection between "angular information" and semantics in this paper?
questions.question_body: The paper motivates OFT by arguing that neuron directions carry semantic information, and it supports this with a toy autoencoder experiment where angular information can almost reconstruct the image while magnitude information cannot. I understand the experiment qualitatively, but I am not sure how much of that transfers to pretrained diffusion model weights. Is the claim that semantics are literally encoded mainly in the angles of weight vectors, or only that angular changes are a good low-level proxy for semantic change during finetuning? I am confused about how strong this assumption is supposed to be.

questions.title: Why is hyperspherical energy defined as $\sum_{i \ne j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$ instead of a direct cosine-similarity quantity?
questions.question_body: The paper discusses hyperspherical similarity using cosine similarity, but then defines the hyperspherical energy of a layer as $\mathrm{HE}(\bm{W}) = \sum_{i \ne j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. I am confused about why this particular inverse-distance form is used. Since for unit vectors the Euclidean distance and cosine angle are related, is this just a monotone reparameterization, or does it have a special property that matters for the theory? Also, what happens numerically if two neurons become very close and a term becomes large?

questions.title: Does preserving hyperspherical energy really preserve semantics, or is it only preserving one scalar summary?
questions.question_body: One part of the paper says a good finetuned model should have minimal difference in hyperspherical energy from the pretrained model. But hyperspherical energy, as defined here, is just one scalar sum over all neuron pairs. Many different neuron configurations could share the same energy. At the same time, the actual OFT parameterization $\bm{W} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0$ is much stronger, because it preserves every pairwise angle exactly. So I am confused about what the real hypothesis is: does the paper rely on preserving the scalar $\mathrm{HE}(\bm{W})$, or on preserving the full pairwise angular geometry induced by a shared orthogonal transform?

questions.title: What expressivity is lost when OFT restricts updates to the form $\bm{W} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0$?
questions.question_body: Compared with standard finetuning, OFT only allows multiplicative updates through an orthogonal matrix. This seems much more restrictive than arbitrary additive updates, and even more structured than LoRA. I understand why that may help preserve pretrained behavior, but I cannot tell what kinds of downstream changes are impossible under this constraint. For example, if the target task requires changing the relative angles between neurons or moving weights outside the span implied by $\bm{W}^0$, does OFT fundamentally fail? Is there a clean way to describe the function class reachable by OFT versus LoRA?

questions.title: Why does the paper say the Cayley parameterization only gives determinant $1$, and does excluding reflections matter?
questions.question_body: The paper parameterizes the orthogonal matrix as $\bm{R} = (\bm{I} + \bm{Q})(\bm{I} - \bm{Q})^{-1}$ for a skew-symmetric matrix $\bm{Q} = -\bm{Q}^\top$, and then says this only produces orthogonal matrices with determinant $1$. My confusion is twofold. First, why exactly does this parameterization exclude determinant $-1$ matrices? Second, since the earlier discussion allowed both rotations and reflections as valid ways to preserve hyperspherical energy, what is lost by restricting to the special orthogonal group? Could there be finetuning directions that require a reflection?

questions.title: How justified is the COFT step that replaces $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \le \epsilon$ with a constraint on $\bm{Q}$?
questions.question_body: In COFT, the paper adds a deviation constraint $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \le \epsilon$ and then argues that, using the Cayley transform and a Neumann-series approximation, this can be turned into a constraint $\|\bm{Q}\| \le \epsilon'$ on the skew-symmetric matrix $\bm{Q}$. I am struggling with this step. Since $\bm{R} = (\bm{I} + \bm{Q})(\bm{I} - \bm{Q})^{-1}$ is nonlinear in $\bm{Q}$, is the new constraint only approximate? Under what norm and under what conditions on $\bm{Q}$ does this really guarantee that $\bm{R}$ stays within the desired radius of the identity?

questions.title: Why does a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix still preserve hyperspherical energy of the full neurons?
questions.question_body: To reduce parameters, the paper replaces a full orthogonal matrix with a block-diagonal one, $\bm{R} = \mathrm{diag}(\bm{R}_1, \ldots, \bm{R}_r)$. I understand that such an $\bm{R}$ is still orthogonal if each block is orthogonal, but intuitively it feels like it only rotates coordinates inside each block and never mixes features across blocks. So why does this still preserve the hyperspherical energy of the whole neuron vectors exactly? Is the only effect of block structure to reduce expressivity, while the pairwise-angle preservation remains mathematically exact?

questions.title: Is the OFT-versus-LoRA parameter-efficiency comparison in the paper using a fair scaling regime?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that if $r = r' = \alpha d$, then OFT can have parameter complexity $\mathcal{O}(d)$ while LoRA has $\mathcal{O}(d^2 + dn)$. I am having trouble interpreting this comparison, because in practice LoRA ranks are often kept as small constants rather than scaling linearly with $d$. On the other hand, OFT's block count $r$ is also a structural hyperparameter rather than a direct analogue of rank. Is there a principled way to compare the two methods at equal expressive capacity, or is this complexity argument mainly illustrative?

questions.title: Why should OFT converge faster than LoRA if both are parameter-efficient finetuning methods?
questions.question_body: The paper repeatedly claims that OFT and COFT converge faster and more smoothly than LoRA and other baselines. The explanation given is that changing neuron directions is more semantically effective, and that optimization on a smooth hypersphere manifold may be easier. I can follow this intuitively, but I do not see a concrete optimization reason. Is there a more formal argument for why orthogonal updates should improve conditioning or gradient flow here, or is this mostly an empirical observation from the experiments?

questions.title: Why does re-scaled OFT still count as preserving the important structure if it allows arbitrary positive per-neuron scaling?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a re-scaled OFT variant with forward pass $\bm{z} = (\bm{R}\bm{W}^0\bm{D})^\top \bm{x}$, where $\bm{D}$ is a positive diagonal matrix. I understand that scaling each neuron does not change hyperspherical energy because normalization removes magnitudes. But from the network's forward-pass perspective, changing magnitudes can still strongly affect activations and therefore generation. So I am confused about the interpretation: if the key preservation property is unchanged hyperspherical energy, why does adding unrestricted scaling not undermine the same stability argument?
